issues.legal_issue: An eviction order is not invalid merely because the lease and eviction proceeding use the name of a non-juristic business where the lease was made on behalf of an identifiable legal entity, the individual occupant was not the tenant, and the relevant parties were not prejudiced by the entity’s omission as a formal party.
material_facts: The lease was signed by the individual occupant on behalf of a business name and was for the occupant’s residence as the business’s general manager.
The courts below found that the business’s legal corporate owner was the tenant and that the individual occupant was not the tenant.
The corporate owner accepted that it owned the business, and the parties knew of that relationship.
The corporate owner and business were not prejudiced by the finding that the individual was not the lessee or by the corporate owner not being made a formal party.
The courts below found grounds for eviction, including non-payment of rent, and the trial court found a bona fide need for the premises.
issues.conclusion: The technical objection that the business name was not a juristic person and that its legal owner was not made a formal party did not warrant setting aside the eviction order.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(i) and 13 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, concern the identity of the tenant and eviction; Order 30 Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure and section 3(42) of the General Clauses Act were discussed in relation to suits involving business names. The Court referred to Modi Vanaspati Manufacturing Company v. Katihar Jute Mills, Rajendra Prasad Oil Mills v. Chunni Devi, M.K.M. Moosa Bhai Amin v. Rajasthan Textile Mills, and Educational Supplies Depot v. Vithoba High School, which addressed proceedings involving assumed business names or non-juristic entities. The decision rested on the findings that the individual was not the tenant, the legal corporate owner was identifiable and accepted its connection to the business, and no relevant party was prejudiced.

rule.if: rent_eviction_proceeding and lease_signed_for_business_name and individual_not_tenant and legal_owner_identifiable and no_party_prejudiced_by_formal_omission

predicates.rent_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding sought eviction of an occupant or tenant from rented premises.
predicates.lease_signed_for_business_name: The lease was signed on behalf of a business name rather than in the individual signatory’s own capacity.
predicates.individual_not_tenant: The courts found that the individual occupant was not the tenant under the lease.
predicates.legal_owner_identifiable: The business name was connected to an identifiable legal entity that was understood to own or operate the business.
predicates.no_party_prejudiced_by_formal_omission: The relevant business and its legal owner were not prejudiced because the legal owner was not formally joined.

issues.definition: When an eviction proceeding concerns a lease made for a business name, the individual signatory is found not to be the tenant, the legal owner is identifiable, and no party is prejudiced by its formal omission, the eviction order is not set aside on that technical ground.

issues.legal_issue: The Court should not interfere under its special appellate jurisdiction with concurrent eviction findings merely to correct a technical legal flaw where interference is not required to prevent manifest injustice or address a substantial question of public importance, while it may shape relief to serve justice.
material_facts: The appeal challenged concurrent findings of the rent authorities and High Court ordering eviction.
The courts below found that rent had not been deposited in accordance with law, and the record supported a bona fide need for the premises.
The lease and party-naming objections were technical, and the Court found no resulting prejudice warranting interference.

The Court considered the length of time and the circumstances of the case and dismissed the appeal while imposing conditions concerning the landlady’s future letting or sale of the premises, execution of the eviction decree, and payment of occupation charges.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere with the eviction findings and dismissed the appeal, but imposed equitable conditions on the landlady and on the appellant’s continued occupation.
issues.legal_principle: Article 136 of the Constitution gives the Court discretionary power that is not an ordinary further appeal. Under Heavy Engineering Corporation Ltd. v. K. Singh and Company and Baigana v. Deputy Collector of Consolidation, the Court need not decide every legal point after leave has been granted and should intervene only where there is a supreme need, such as manifest injustice or a substantial question of public importance. In exercising that power, the Court acts as a court of equity as well as a court of law and must ultimately serve justice.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and concurrent_eviction_findings and technical_flaw_without_prejudice and no_manifest_injustice_or_public_importance and circumstances_support_equitable_conditions

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal brought under the Supreme Court’s discretionary special appellate jurisdiction.
predicates.concurrent_eviction_findings: The lower courts reached consistent findings supporting eviction.
predicates.technical_flaw_without_prejudice: The appellant relied on a technical flaw that did not cause prejudice to a relevant party.
predicates.no_manifest_injustice_or_public_importan: The circumstances disclose neither manifest injustice requiring intervention nor a substantial question of public importance.
predicates.circumstances_support_equitable_conditio: The circumstances, including the demonstrated need for the premises and the passage of time, support conditions designed to serve justice.

issues.definition: When a special-leave appeal challenges concurrent eviction findings on a non-prejudicial technical flaw, no manifest injustice or substantial public importance calls for intervention, and the circumstances support equitable conditions, the appeal is dismissed without disturbing those findings but subject to such conditions.
